ety.text: From Middle English hasel, from Old English hæsl (“hazel, shrub”), from Proto-West Germanic *hasl, from Proto-Germanic *haslaz (“hazel”), from Proto-Indo-European *kóslos (“hazel”). Cognates Cognate with Yola hawlse (“hazel”), Dutch hazel, hazelaar (“hazel”), German Hasel (“hazel”), Vilamovian hozuł (“hazel”), Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, and Swedish hassel (“hazel”), Icelandic hesli (“hazel”), Norwegian Nynorsk hasl, hassel (“hazel”); also Latin corulus, corylus (“hazel”), Irish call, coll (“hazel”), Manx coull (“hazel”), Scottish Gaelic coll (“hazel”), Welsh cyll (“hazel trees”).

senses.d: A tree or shrub of the genus Corylus, bearing edible nuts called hazelnuts or filberts.
ex: The green turf was velvet underfoot. The blackbirds fluted in the hazels there.

senses.d: The nut of the hazel tree.
The wood of a hazelnut tree.
A greenish-brown colour, the colour of a ripe hazelnut.
Freestone.
Of a greenish-brown colour. (often used to refer to eye colour)
ex: The shrewd eyes, more hazel than her son’s but with the same straight brows, were fixed on Clary’s face.
Doolittle had the hazelest eyeballs, the winsomest spinal pelt.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese castanho (“brown”), probably from Latin castaneus (“pertaining to chestnuts”). Cognate with Galician castaño, Mirandese castanho, Asturian castañu, Spanish castaño and Catalan castany. Doublet of castâneo.
From Vulgar Latin *nuceola, from nuceus (“of nuts”), from Latin nux (“nut”). Compare Ligurian nisêua, Sicilian nuzzola, Venetan noxeła, Romansh nitschola, and also French noisette.

From Middle English hasard, from Old French hasart (“a game of dice”) (noun), hasarder (verb), from Arabic اَلزَّهْر (az-zahr, “the dice”). Compare Spanish azar, Portuguese azar.

senses.d: A game of chance played with dice, usually for monetary stakes, popular mainly from 14th c. to 19th c.
ex: [T]here's Harry diets himself—for gaming and is now under a hazard Regimen.
She realized then that, of course, no one was playing hazard. Dice games were technically illegal, and certainly improper.

senses.d: Chance; accident, unpredictability.
ex: I will stand the hazard of the die.
I see animated movies are now managing, by hazard or design, to reflect our contemporary reality more accurately than live-action movies.

senses.d: The risk of some loss or harm; danger, peril, the chance of an adverse outcome.
ex: He encountered the enemy at the hazard of his reputation and life.
Men are led on from one stage of life to another in a condition of the utmost hazard.

senses.d: A situation involving such a risk of harm or loss; (later also) a person or object which poses such a risk, something seen as a source of danger or difficulty.
ex: The video game involves guiding a character on a skateboard past all kinds of hazards.
Quite apart from the gruesome road hazards, snow is awful even when you don't have to travel.

senses.d: Each of the various openings or galleries around the side of a court.
Anything that is hazarded or risked, such as a stake in gambling.
A stroke which results in potting a ball, whether the object ball (winning hazard) or the player's ball (losing hazard).
Something which prevents free striking of the ball, such as a sand or water obstacle.
A cabstand, especially in Dublin.
ex: Mr Bloom went round the corner and passed the drooping nags of the hazard.

senses.d: A problem with the instruction pipeline in CPU microarchitectures when the next instruction cannot execute in the following clock cycle, potentially leading to incorrect results.
To expose to chance; to take a risk.
ex: to be consistent, you ought to be a Chriſtian in temper and practice; for you hazard nothing by a course of evangelical obedience
He hazards his neck to the halter.

senses.d: To risk (something); to venture, incur, or bring on.
ex: I hazarded the loss of whom I loved.

grp.label: to chance; to take a risk

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French hasard, from Old French hasart, from Old Spanish azar, from Arabic اَلزَّهْر (az-zahr, “flowers”), named after a game of dice where the winning side of the die had a flower on it. Compare modern Spanish azar, Italian zara.
